content: 1. Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever (CCHF) is a disease caused by a tick-borne virus, specifically a nairovirus. It is endemic in regions such as Africa, Asia, Southeastern Europe, and the Middle East. 2. The clinical presentation of CCHF occurs in two phases: the pre-hemorrhagic phase and the hemorrhagic phase. 3. The pre-hemorrhagic phase begins with non-specific prodromal symptoms, including high fever, muscle pain (myalgia), headache, nausea, abdominal pain, and cardiovascular signs such as bradycardia and hypotension. 4. The hemorrhagic phase is typically brief and involves symptoms such as petechiae, conjunctival hemorrhage, nosebleeds (epistaxis), coughing up blood (hemoptysis), vomiting blood (hematemesis), and commonly bruising (ecchymosis), black tarry stools (melena), blood in the urine (hematuria), and abnormal uterine bleeding (metrorrhagia). 5. The case fatality rate for CCHF ranges from 10% to 40%, with death often resulting from multi-organ failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and circulatory shock. 6. The primary mode of transmission to humans is through tick bites or direct contact with the blood of infected ticks or animals, such as livestock. Human-to-human transmission can occur through contact with blood, secretions, or other body fluids of infected individuals. 7. In healthcare settings, healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) of CCHF have been reported due to breaches in infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, such as improper sterilization of equipment, reuse of syringes, contamination of medical supplies, and inadequate use of personal protective equipment (PPE). 8. A review of 158 HAI cases of CCHF from 1958 to 2016 revealed that most cases occurred through percutaneous (34%) and cutaneous (22%) exposures, as well as contact with contaminated surfaces (8%). 9. The incubation period of CCHF depends on the mode of transmission. After a tick bite, the incubation period is typically 1 to 3 days, with a maximum of 9 days. Following contact with infected blood or tissues, the incubation period is usually 5 to 6 days, with a maximum of 13 days. 10. IPC measures for suspected or confirmed CCHF cases are based on standard and transmission-based precautions to prevent or control infection transmission, ensuring the safety of patients, healthcare workers, and visitors. 11. Patients with suspected or confirmed CCHF should be immediately isolated in single-bed rooms. If single rooms are unavailable, cohort isolation of laboratory-confirmed cases may be considered under specific criteria. 12. Aerosol-generating procedures on CCHF patients must be performed in airborne infection isolation rooms with adequate ventilation (minimum 160 liters per second or 6–12 air changes per hour). If such rooms are unavailable, ensure cross-ventilation and use fans to exhaust air outdoors. 13. Healthcare workers must use appropriate PPE, including fluid-resistant gowns, gloves, fit-tested respirators, and eye protection, when caring for CCHF patients or performing aerosol-generating procedures. 14. Visitors and caregivers must wear PPE and maintain at least 1 meter of physical distance from CCHF patients. They should be instructed on hand hygiene and the proper donning and doffing of PPE. 15. Environmental cleaning and disinfection in patient care areas should be performed at least twice daily using detergent and disinfectants such as 0.5% sodium hypochlorite solution. 16. Patient care equipment should be disposable or dedicated to individual patients. Reusable equipment must be cleaned and disinfected or sterilized according to manufacturer instructions and national or international standards. 17. Soiled linens from CCHF patients should be placed in leakproof, clearly labeled bags and handled separately. Laundry staff must wear PPE, and heavily soiled linens should be disposed of as infectious waste. 18. Hand hygiene must be performed before and after patient contact, after removing PPE, and after contact with potentially contaminated surfaces or equipment. 19. Healthcare workers should avoid unnecessary movement of suspected or confirmed CCHF patients. If transport is required, ensure transmission-based precautions are maintained, and patients with respiratory symptoms should wear well-fitted medical masks. 20. Consistent application of environmental controls, including cleaning, disinfection, and waste management, is essential to prevent the spread of CCHF in healthcare settings.
